explanation.body: The mean kinetic energy per particle is $\frac32 kT$. The neon-to-argon ratio is therefore $T_X/T_Y=1$ because the gases are at the same temperature.

perOption.A: Uses the particle mass ratio as the energy ratio.
perOption.C: Uses the pressure ratio as the energy ratio.
perOption.D: Combines the pressure ratio with the inverse mass ratio, although neither enters the mean energy at fixed temperature.

difficultyReason: The two temperatures can be compared directly using one kinetic-theory relation.
misconception: Mean kinetic energy scales with particle mass or pressure.

explanation.body: Kinetic theory gives $p=\frac13(Nm/V)\langle c^2\rangle=\frac13\rho\langle c^2\rangle$. Thus $c_{\mathrm{rms}}=\sqrt{3p/\rho}=\sqrt{3(150\times10^3)/0.178}\approx1600\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This speed is too small to give the stated pressure at the given density.
perOption.B: This speed is too small when the pressure is entered as 150,000 Pa.
perOption.C: Using a factor of 2 in place of 3 in the speed formula gives about this value.

difficultyReason: The calculation requires substituting mass density and converting kilopascals to pascals.
misconception: Using the wrong pressure units or kinetic-theory factor.

explanation.body: Along FG, $pV$ is constant, so the ideal gas undergoes an isothermal expansion. Its temperature stays constant, so its internal energy does not change.

perOption.A: The gas does net work over the cycle and returns to its initial internal energy, so it gains net heat.
perOption.C: At constant volume the gas does zero work, so its increase in internal energy comes from heat gained.
perOption.D: The areas under EF and GH differ, so the work magnitudes differ.

difficultyReason: The cycle requires interpreting pressure–volume areas, temperature and heat transfer.
misconception: Confusing heat transfer with work or internal-energy change.

explanation.body: Q is moving downwards on a downward slope, so the wave profile is travelling to the left. Shift the profile a little to the left and compare the displacements at the two possible positions of P, each $\frac78\lambda$ from Q. At the left position P is below equilibrium and moves downwards, while at the right position it is above equilibrium and also moves downwards.

perOption.A: At the possible position with positive displacement, P moves downwards.
perOption.B: Neither possible position is at a crest or trough, where the transverse velocity would be zero.
perOption.C: Neither possible position is at a zero crossing.
perOption.D: Correct. This applies to the position to the left of Q.

difficultyReason: The student must infer wave travel from the motion at Q and check both possible positions of P.
misconception: Confusing particle motion with wave propagation.
transcription:
This diagram shows the displacement-distance graph of a transverse wave at time, $t=0$. Taking upwards as positive, point Q is a point on the wave and is travelling downwards at $t=0$. Another point P is $\frac78$ of a wavelength from point Q.

[Displacement is plotted vertically against distance along wave horizontally. Three sinusoidal cycles start at zero with a rising slope. Q is marked at the descending zero crossing after the second crest.]

Which of the following descriptions shows a possible displacement and direction of velocity of point P?

Option | displacement | direction of velocity
A | positive | positive
B | positive | 0
C | 0 | negative
D | negative | negative

explanation.body: P and S are separated by one complete period plus a quarter-period. The complete period contributes $2\pi$ and leaves the same phase, so the phase difference within a cycle is $2\pi(T/4)/T=\pi/2\ \mathrm{rad}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The points differ in phase by a quarter-cycle.
perOption.B: The acceleration magnitude is greatest at T because the displacement magnitude is greatest there.
perOption.C: Potential energy is greatest at the turning point T and is smaller at Q.
perOption.D: Kinetic energy is greatest at the equilibrium crossing R and is smaller at Q.

issues: The school uses a quarter-period separation modulo one period. The plotted elapsed time is five quarter-periods.
difficultyReason: The graph gives the phase once the student accounts for the intervening complete cycle.
misconception: Reading zero velocity at a turning point as zero acceleration.
transcription:
The graph below shows the variation with time $t$ of the displacement $x$ of a simple harmonic oscillator oscillating horizontally.

[The sinusoidal curve starts at the origin with positive slope. P marks the first crest and Q lies on the following descending positive-displacement segment. R is the next rising zero crossing, S the following descending zero crossing and T the trough after S.]

Which statement is correct?

A The phase difference between P and S is $\frac{\pi}{2}\ \mathrm{rad}$.
B The acceleration at T is zero.
C The potential energy of the oscillator is larger at Q compared to T.
D The kinetic energy of the oscillator is larger at Q compared to R.

explanation.body: The tube behaves as a pipe of length $L$ with one closed end and one open end. Its fundamental has $\lambda=4L$ and $f=80\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The first and second overtones have wavelengths $4L/3$ and $4L/5$, giving $240\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and $400\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Only odd multiples of the fundamental are possible, including $9f=720\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: 160 Hz and 320 Hz are even multiples of the fundamental.
perOption.B: All three frequencies are even multiples of the fundamental.
perOption.C: Correct. All three frequencies are odd multiples of 80 Hz.
perOption.D: 320 Hz and 480 Hz are even multiples of the fundamental.

difficultyReason: The node and antinode boundary conditions determine which multiples of the fundamental are allowed.
misconception: Allowing even harmonics in a pipe with one closed end.

explanation.body: The charge is the triangular area under the current–time graph, $Q=\frac12(1.0)(2.0\times3600)=3600\ \mathrm C$. The energy transferred is $QV=3600(6.0)=21\,600\ \mathrm J$, which rounds to $22\,000\ \mathrm J$.

perOption.A: Converting the two hours to 120 minutes and using 120 as seconds gives this value.
perOption.B: Using 120 as seconds and treating the current as constant at 1.0 A gives this value.
perOption.D: Uses the initial current for the whole interval, doubling the triangular area.

difficultyReason: The student converts hours to seconds, reads the graph area and uses it to calculate energy.
misconception: Using the peak current for the whole interval.

explanation.body: At $2.0\ \mathrm{mA}$, the graph shows $V_Q=8.0\ \mathrm V$ and $V_P=4.0\ \mathrm V$. Since $P=IV$ and the currents are equal, Q dissipates twice as much power as P.

perOption.A: Q has the characteristic of a semiconductor diode, whereas a filament's resistance rises as it heats.
perOption.B: Above the nonzero crossing, Q carries more current at the same voltage, giving it a lower resistance.
perOption.D: At the nonzero intersection both components have the same voltage and current, so their resistances are equal.

difficultyReason: The graph must be read at a specified current and interpreted using power and resistance relations.
misconception: Treating the local graph slope as the reciprocal of resistance.

explanation.body: The parallel pair $R_2$ and $R_3$ has resistance $(1/R+1/R)^{-1}=R/2$, so the supply current is $I=E/(R+R/2)$. The p.d. across $R_1$ is $IR=2E/3$, leaving $E/3$ across $R_2$. Since both resistors have resistance $R$, the power ratio is $(2E/3)^2/(E/3)^2=4$.

perOption.A: Assumes the identical resistors have equal potential differences.
perOption.B: Uses the voltage ratio directly without squaring it.
perOption.D: Uses the full battery voltage for the numerator, giving a voltage ratio of 3.

difficultyReason: The student must reduce the parallel pair and use the resulting voltage division to find a power ratio.
misconception: Assuming equal resistances dissipate equal power.

explanation.body: At balance, the current through the secondary cell is zero. Its terminal p.d. $V_{AB}$ remains equal to its e.m.f. when its internal resistance decreases, so the wire length $L_{XZ}$ needed to match that p.d. is unchanged.

perOption.A: A lower driver e.m.f. reduces the p.d. across XY, so XZ must be longer to match the secondary e.m.f.
perOption.B: A larger secondary e.m.f. requires a larger p.d. across XZ and hence a longer balance length.
perOption.C: The series resistor lowers the p.d. across XY, so a longer length is required to match the secondary e.m.f.

issues: A–C increase the required balance length provided the new balance point still lies on the wire.
difficultyReason: Solving the question requires identifying the null condition and how the driver circuit sets the wire's potential gradient.
misconception: Assuming internal resistance changes terminal voltage even at zero current.

explanation.body: Electric potential decreases in the direction of the electric field. Moving against the field therefore takes you towards higher potential.

perOption.A: Potential decreases when moving along the field line in the arrow's direction.
perOption.C: Field direction alone does not imply decreasing field strength, as a uniform field shows.
perOption.D: Field direction alone does not imply increasing field strength, as a uniform field shows.

difficultyReason: This follows directly from the relationship between field direction and potential gradient.
misconception: Confusing potential with electric field magnitude.

explanation.body: The opposite magnetic forces on the two sides form a couple with perpendicular separation $d=L\cos30^\circ$. With $N$ turns, the torque is $\tau=NBILd=10(2.0)(15)(5.0/100)(5.0/100)\cos30^\circ\approx0.65\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the sine projection and halves the couple's torque again.
perOption.B: Uses half the perpendicular separation while counting only one force.
perOption.C: Uses the sine projection for the separation of the forces.

difficultyReason: The student must identify the magnetic couple and project the coil width to find the perpendicular separation.
misconception: Using the coil angle to project the wrong lever arm.

explanation.body: The coil axis is parallel to the field, so the field is normal to the area enclosed by the coil. The magnitude of the induced e.m.f. is $NA|\Delta B|/\Delta t=120(0.070)(80-20)\times10^{-3}/4.0=0.126\ \mathrm V\approx130\ \mathrm{mV}$.

perOption.A: Treats the coil's axis as if it lay in the coil's plane and assumes zero flux.
perOption.B: Calculates the induced e.m.f. for just one turn.
perOption.D: Uses the change in flux linkage without dividing by the 4.0 s interval.

difficultyReason: The student must determine the field orientation and divide the flux-linkage change by time.
misconception: Using change in flux linkage without dividing by time.

explanation.body: During the conducting half-period, the mean of $V^2$ is $V_0^2/2$, giving an area of $(V_0^2/2)(T/2)=V_0^2T/4$ under the $V^2$–time graph over one period. The r.m.s. voltage is $\sqrt{(V_0^2T/4)/T}=V_0/2=100\ \mathrm V$, so $V_0=200\ \mathrm V$.

perOption.A: Halves the given r.m.s. value instead of doubling it to find the peak.
perOption.B: Divides the r.m.s. voltage by the ordinary sinusoidal conversion factor when finding the peak.
perOption.C: Uses the ordinary sinusoidal peak-to-r.m.s. ratio while ignoring the zero half-cycle.

difficultyReason: The student must average the squared voltage over the full period, including the zero half-cycle.
misconception: Applying the unrectified sinusoidal RMS formula to a half-wave waveform.

explanation.body: The photoelectric equation is $hf=eV_s+\Phi$, where $V_s$ is the stopping voltage magnitude. The graph gives $V_{s,x}<V_{s,y}$, so $f_x<f_y$. With the usual assumption that higher saturation current indicates greater intensity, $i_x<i_y$ gives $I_x<I_y$.

perOption.A: The stopping voltage magnitude and saturation current are both smaller for x.
perOption.B: The smaller saturation current for x indicates lower intensity in the model used here.
perOption.C: The smaller stopping voltage magnitude for x indicates lower frequency.

issues: The intensity comparison assumes a comparable photocell response. Saturation current alone measures collected photoelectrons per unit time and cannot determine intensity for arbitrary frequency-dependent quantum efficiencies.
difficultyReason: The student must distinguish the roles of stopping voltage and saturation current.
misconception: Using saturation current to infer frequency.
transcription:
The figure shows the variation of the photoelectric current $i$ with voltage $V$ between the electrodes in a photocell for two different radiations, x and y.

[Two curves show current $i$ against electrode voltage $V$. Both rise from zero at negative voltages and level off at positive voltages. Curve y starts at a more negative voltage and levels off at a higher current than curve x. The origin is labelled 0.]

The intensity and the frequency of radiation x are $I_x$ and $f_x$ while the intensity and the frequency of radiation y are $I_y$ and $f_y$. Which of the following shows the relationship between the intensities and frequencies of x and y?

A $I_x>I_y$, $f_x>f_y$
B $I_x>I_y$, $f_x<f_y$
C $I_x<I_y$, $f_x>f_y$
D $I_x<I_y$, $f_x<f_y$
